title: Malta Year 8 Math Chapter 13 — Graphs
question: How do you read and plot points, name horizontal and vertical lines, draw a straight-line graph and read a real-life graph?
intro:
Chapter 13 works with coordinates and graphs.

**Chapter 13 has four parts:**

- 13.1 Coordinates
- 13.2 Horizontal and vertical lines
- 13.3 Straight-line graphs
- 13.4 Real-life graphs

**By the end of the chapter:**

- read and plot points in all four quarters
- name a line \(x = a\) or \(y = b\)
- make a table of values and draw the line
- read a conversion graph and a distance–time graph

questions.title: Read a point: across, then up
questions.prompt:
- A point is written \((x, y)\).
- Start at 0.
- Go **across** \(x\), then **up** \(y\).

**Examples:**

- **a)** point A

- **b)** point B

- **c)** point C

- **d)** point D
steps:
**d)** 3 across, 0 up:

\[\boxed{(3, 0)}\]

Not \((3, 2)\) for A: across comes first.
questions.figure_alt: A grid from 0 to 6 across and 0 to 5 up with A (2, 3), B (5, 1), C (0, 4) and D (3, 0); arrows show across first, then up.

questions.title: Four quarters: negative coordinates
questions.prompt:
- Left of 0, \(x\) is **negative**.
- Below 0, \(y\) is **negative**.

**Examples:**

- **a)** point E

- **b)** point F

- **c)** point G

- **d)** point H
steps:
**d)** 5 left, 0 up:

\[\boxed{(-5, 0)}\]

Not \((2, -3)\) for E: still across first, then up or down.
questions.figure_alt: A grid from −6 to 6 across and −5 to 5 up with E (−3, 2), F (−2, −4), G (4, −1) and H (−5, 0).

questions.title: Vertical x = …, horizontal y = …
questions.prompt:
- On a **vertical** line every point has the same \(x\): the line is \(x = \ldots\).
- On a **horizontal** line every point has the same \(y\): the line is \(y = \ldots\).

**Examples:**

- **a)** the line through \((3, 1)\) and \((3, 4)\)

- **b)** the line through \((-1, -2)\) and \((4, -2)\)

- **c)** the \(y\)-axis

- **d)** the line through \((-4, 5)\) and \((2, 5)\)
steps:
**c)** every point on it has:

\[\begin{aligned} x &= 0 \\ & \boxed{x = 0} \end{aligned}\]

**d)** \(y\) is 5 both times:

\[\boxed{y = 5}\]

Not \(y = 3\) for a): the 3 is the \(x\) that stays the same, so \(x = 3\) (and the line stands up).
questions.figure_alt: A grid with the vertical line x = 3 through (3, 1) and (3, 4), and the horizontal line y = −2 through (−1, −2) and (4, −2).

questions.title: Is the point on the line?
questions.prompt:
- Put the \(x\) of the point into the rule.
- If you get its \(y\), the point is **on** the line.

**Examples:**

- **a)** \((2, 5)\) and \(y = 2x + 1\)

- **b)** \((3, 6)\) and \(y = 2x + 1\)

- **c)** \((0, 1)\) and \(y = 2x + 1\)

- **d)** \((-1, -1)\) and \(y = 2x + 1\)
steps:
**d)**

\[2\times(-1) + 1 = -1\] \(\boxed{\text{on the line}}\)

Times first, then add.
questions.figure_alt: The line y = 2x + 1 with the points a (2, 5), c (0, 1) and d (−1, −1) on it, and b (3, 6) just off it.

questions.title: Table of values, then plot
questions.prompt:
Pick some \(x\) values, work out each \(y\) with the rule, then plot the pairs \((x, y)\) and join them: a straight line.

**Examples:**

- **a)** \(y = x + 2\) at \(x = 0\)

- **b)** \(y = x + 2\) at \(x = 1\)

- **c)** \(y = x + 2\) at \(x = 2\)

- **d)** \(y = x + 2\) at \(x = 3\)
steps:
**d)**

\[\begin{aligned} y &= 3 + 2 \\ &= \boxed{5} \end{aligned}\] plot \((3, 5)\)

If one point is off the straight line, check that \(y\) again.
questions.figure_alt: A table x = 0, 1, 2, 3 and y = 2, 3, 4, 5, and the four points plotted on a grid and joined: the line y = x + 2.

questions.title: Read the line: y from x, x from y
questions.prompt:
- To find \(y\): go **up** from \(x\) to the line, then **across** to the \(y\)-axis.
- To find \(x\): go across from \(y\) to the line, then down.

**Examples:**

- **a)** \(y\) when \(x = 2\)

- **b)** \(y\) when \(x = 4\)

- **c)** \(x\) when \(y = 5\)

- **d)** \(x\) when \(y = 1\)
questions.figure_alt: The line y = 2x − 1 on a grid; a dashed path goes up from x = 2 to the line and across to y = 3.

questions.title: Conversion graph
questions.prompt:
- A straight line through 0 changes one unit into another.
- Go up from one axis to the line, then across.

**Examples:**

- **a)** 16 km in miles

- **b)** 32 km in miles

- **c)** 15 miles in km

- **d)** 5 miles in km
steps:
**d)** across from 5, down:

\[\boxed{8 \text{ km}}\]

Check with \(8 \text{ km} = 5 \text{ miles}\): 16 km is twice 8, so twice 5.
questions.figure_alt: A straight conversion line from 0 to 40 km = 25 miles; a dashed path goes up from 16 km and across to 10 miles.

questions.title: Distance–time graph
questions.prompt:
- Time goes across, distance goes up.
- A **flat** part means the bus is **stopped**: time passes, the distance stays.

**Examples:**

- **a)** how far after 20 minutes?

- **b)** how long is the stop?

- **c)** how far is the whole trip?

- **d)** how long does the whole trip take?
steps:
**c)** the top of the graph:

\[\boxed{18 \text{ km}}\]

**d)** the end of the graph:

\[\boxed{50 \text{ minutes}}\]

Not 30 km for c): the flat part adds no distance.
questions.figure_alt: A distance–time graph of a bus trip: 10 km in 20 minutes, flat from 20 to 30 minutes, then up to 18 km at 50 minutes.
